### 2026-07-13 (main) — July 9 ThetaData backfill closed + rebuild_catalog() production bug found/fixed (4 bugs)
Closes #22 (missing 2026-07-09 ThetaData options-chain snapshot). Data collection succeeded early (all 50 roots, verified on disk), but closing this out required chasing a real pre-existing production bug in datacollector/storage.py's rebuild_catalog() -- the backfill script's final step, called after every one-off backfill and by the nightly ThetaEodDaily job.

Four distinct bugs found and fixed in sequence, each only surfacing after fixing the last:
1. Original: rebuild_catalog() embedded all ~312k warehouse file paths as one literal SQL array in a single CREATE VIEW ... read_parquet(..., union_by_name=true) statement. Confirmed via real benchmarks (2k/20k/100k file scales) to scale superlinearly -- killed after 52 min with no completion against the real 311,988-file warehouse. (Matches a prior undiagnosed symptom: a 2026-06-27 commit message already noted this function 'hard-crashing the interpreter' at ~102k files -- same root cause, never fixed until now.)
2. Fix attempt 1 (chunking into bounded ~5,000-file views) hit a second bug: the manifest-table bulk write used con.executemany() to upsert ~312k rows one at a time -- killed after 46+ min with no completion.
3. Fix attempt 2 (bulk DataFrame-backed insert) surfaced a resume-robustness gap: a kill between the manifest commit and the per-chunk view-build loop could leave some chunk views un-built with no way to detect it on a later no-op call. Fixed by detecting chunks whose _catalog_chunks row has no live view.
4. The real remaining wall (not anticipated going in): UNION ALL BY NAME over many chunk views is NOT cheap regardless of file count -- DuckDB re-binds each chunk's full read_parquet(union_by_name=true) definition on every reference, compounding to ~O(n^2) in chunk count (measured 4s/10s/34s/140s at 2/4/8/16 chunks). Fixed by forcing one consistent schema across all chunks up front (an explicit read_parquet(schema=...) derived from a representative file, forcing the real open_interest double/int64 type drift found during diagnosis to DOUBLE in both file orderings), so the union becomes plain positional UNION ALL -- confirmed linear (0.29s @ 16 chunks vs 140s before).

Real measured result: full bootstrap rebuild against the actual 311,988-file warehouse now takes 16.9 seconds (was: never completes). Independently verified (not just taken on faith): queried the rebuilt catalog directly and confirmed 187,298 rows for 2026-07-09 across exactly 50 roots; ran the datacollector test suite myself (39 passed, 2 pre-existing unrelated argv-script collection errors, confirmed not caused by this change); confirmed both commits exist and no orphaned processes were left running.

Commits: 40b4a30 (storage.py fix + test_storage.py), ada471c (backfill_20260709.py, one-off script committed for the record, same convention as backfill_20260626.py).

### 2026-07-10 (s8-simulator-abort-2026-07-10) — S8 mechanical simulator: root cause isolated via real-trade replication, then ABORTED by Andrew; pivoted same session to regime-bucketing the known real window
Followed up on open item #18 (mechanical simulator FAILED calibration). Built a deterministic replication test: replayed all 1,222 strict TAT-matched REAL trades (real date+time+template, no invented schedule) through the simulator's per-trade engine and diffed simulated vs real strike/credit/P&L. Findings, in order isolated: (1) strike selection accurate (median ~5pt diff both legs). (2) settlement-trade P&L accurate (mean diff +$70/trade, matches real 79.4% win rate on that subset). (3) B2/long-leg-policy confound RULED OUT -- reran short-leg-only (real short_fifo_pnl vs sim short-leg mechanics, ignoring the long leg entirely, since B2 does not touch the short leg) and got nearly the identical aggregate gap as the whole-position comparison (+$41,202 real vs -$43,734 sim), so B2 diverging from real long-leg handling was never the driver. (4) warehouse data quality RULED OUT -- cross-checked the two most extreme stop-exit mismatches (2026-03-09, 2025-10-14) against the underlying spot-estimate path AND 4 neighboring strikes at the same minute; both moves were coherent across strikes and correlated with a genuine spot move, not isolated bad ticks. (5) stop-trigger CLASSIFICATION is accurate -- 94.8% of the 503 trades the simulator flagged as 'stop' really were real losers (mean real loss -$243/contract on that group). (6) The isolated remaining bug: stop-exit FILL MAGNITUDE on those correctly-classified trades runs ~2.1x too punishing (sim mean -$508 vs real mean -$243 on the same 503 trades). The 13.6x-half-spread slippage constant's aggregate median roughly matches real data (13.79x measured), so the gap likely comes from applying that multiplier at the exact stressed trigger-minute (when the half-spread is itself already elevated) rather than the constant's central value being wrong -- not fully resolved, two candidate explanations (fill-price-at-stress-moment vs trigger-timing precision) were left unpicked. Andrew's call at that point: ABORT the mechanical-simulator/2022-2026-extension approach entirely, not fix-and-continue. Rationale: every component (spot estimate, strike selection, entry timing, fill model) has only ever been checked against the ONE period with real ground truth (2025-2026) -- even a fixed version extending trust to genuinely novel years (2022-2024) would be an unverifiable leap, a curve-fit risk baked into the whole approach, not just this one bug. Session cost (hours of diagnostic chasing) was also disproportionate to the payoff. Pivoted same session to a much cheaper test of the same underlying worry (is S8's edge concentrated in one type of day): regime-bucketed the REAL known 236-day window using S0's EXISTING FROZEN regime engine (strategies/parts/regime.py -- market_health_score + apply_hysteresis, no new thresholds) joined to the already-existing real daily P&L series (british_ic/alpha_vs_beta_daily_series.csv, built in an earlier session). Zero synthetic execution -- no strike selection, no fill model, no spot estimation. Result: S8 profitable in 4 of 5 regime buckets, covering 212 of 236 days (90%) -- RiskOn +$69,077/101d, RiskOnNarrowing +$64,894/89d, Defensive +$6,104/12d, CapitalPreservation +$8,358/10d (highest per-day mean of any bucket -- the tail-hedge thesis holding up, not just one lucky crash day). One real soft spot: Caution regime, -$9,450/24d. Totals reconcile exactly to the previously-published headline (+$138,981 computed vs +$138,982 documented; +$42,765 actual matches exactly), a strong sanity check the daily series and join are correct. Caveat: extreme-regime buckets are thin (n=10-12) -- this shows the edge isn't fragile to the regime diversity that occurred WITHIN the one known year, it does not prove survival of a genuine multi-year bear or 2008-style event. Left uncommitted: british_ic/s8_mechanical_simulator.py + SIMULATOR_STAGE_B_PROGRESS.md (prior session's probability-fix attempt, now moot given the abort decision) and 3 new untracked diagnostic scripts (s8_replication_test.py, s8_short_leg_only_diag.py, s8_real_slippage_check.py) documenting this session's isolation work -- not committed, Andrew's call whether to preserve for the record or discard.

### 2026-07-10 (theta-watchdog-hardening) — ThetaTerminalWatchdog hardened: daily-daemon design replaced (2026-07-09 11h52m watchdog-death incident)
Root-caused the 07-09 EOD alarm flood: ThetaEodDaily's 5:30pm forward-collector aborted instantly ('Theta Terminal not reachable'), losing that day's full options-chain snapshot, because the ThetaData terminal was down and theta_terminal_watchdog.py itself (a single long-lived daemon woken once/day at 6am + logon) had silently died sometime after 09:00:41 -- nothing noticed for 11h52m since the daily trigger's singleton lock correctly saw a prior process as 'still alive' each morning; once that one process died there was no supervisor for the supervisor. FAILURE (large detour, do not trust or build on without fresh diagnosis -- see item #18):
Andrew asked to test S8's rules against a much longer history (2022-2026, ~4.5yr of real SPXW
1-min data confirmed on disk) instead of just the known 1-year real-fills window, for more regime
coverage. Required building a from-scratch mechanical simulator (independently re-deriving trades
from raw market data using the same entry-timing/strike-selection/stop/B2 rules, not reconstructing
from real account fills). Commits: d3374ba (simulator skeleton), 77693a5 (empirical entry-schedule
rebuild), 044d93e (Stage-B template comment polish), ed6ff50 (29x performance fix), 501dc24
(calibration-compare + extended-run scripts).

Calibration against the KNOWN 2025-2026 real window (the only way to sanity-check before trusting
the simulator on 2022-2024 where there's no ground truth) came back badly wrong. First attempt:
-$1,440,129 total sim P&L vs the real account's +$138,982 -- traced to entries firing 7x too often
per day (76.5/day vs real 11.0/day) because a schedule-derivation step treated "this time-slot
appeared on X% of historical days" as "fires every day" instead of "fires with probability X%."
Fixed (converted to a real per-slot empirical firing probability, deterministically seeded per
date/template/slot) and re-run on the full 247-day window: trade frequency improved a lot
(15.1/day, much closer to real 11.0/day) but total P&L was STILL negative (-$233,203 vs the real
+$138,982) and the stop rate barely moved (39.8% vs the original 40.4%) -- the frequency fix was
real and necessary but not sufficient; a deeper, still-undiagnosed mismatch remains.

Late in the session Andrew corrected a wrong assumption that had been driving the diagnosis: the
TAT system is a FULLY AUTOMATED algorithmic program (not a human making daily discretionary calls),
which means the real explanation for why any given scheduled slot only fires on 73-85% of its
"eligible" days is a discoverable MECHANICAL rule (an IV filter, a capital/position constraint,
something in the data) -- not human judgment, and not something to model as a random probability
draw the way the fix did. This reframes the whole failure: the probability-weighted-draw fix was
itself likely the wrong model, not just an incomplete one. A further open question, never
resolved: whether the SAME automated system also controls the long leg's exit (in which case "B2"
isn't a proposed correction, it's us discovering an already-existing real rule we haven't correctly
identified) or whether the long-leg exit is a separate/different process (in which case the
existing B2 characterization stands). Session ended here at Andrew's request to stop and wrap up,
without resolving this. See conductor items #18 (simulator) and #19 (long-leg-exit question).
